To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the size distribution of the nuclei formed in a short nucleation pulse is a universal function of the dimensionless parameter zeta proportional to the size difference between the nuclei and the maximum size reached at the end of the nucleation process.

the distribution of nuclei created during a nucleation pulse is strongly asymmetric with a near-flat top in the case of a long nucleation pulse, while it acquires a distinct peak at r = rmax(t) for a short nucleation pulse, and the distribution is independent of the pulse width in both cases, and the peak value rmax(t) is proportional to the square root of the pulse width.

the distribution of particles formed by nucleation in a finite-time pulse is strongly non-monotonic, with an asymmetric shape, and is determined by two dimension-less parameters: the ratio of the critical nuclei radii and the ratio of the growth and nucleation times.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the size distribution of nuclei produced in a nucleation-pulse process.
the analysis of the nucleation-growth processes in which the supersatuation is abruptly changed after nucleation has been allowed to occur during a finite time.
the study of the nucleation and growth processes in the framework of the Turnbull-Fisher and Zeldovich-Fenkel theories.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the size distribution of nucleated particles in a nucleation-pulse experiment is determined by two parameters, lambda and Lambda, which are the dimensionless duration of the nucleation-pulse and the ratio of the critical radii of nuclei formed in the nucleation-pulses and after its termination, respectively.
the distribution of nuclei produced in a finite time interval is strongly dependent upon the duration and the degree of supersaturation.
nucleation pulses are a powerful tool for the study of nucleation and growth processes, and the present analysis provides the theoretical background for their application to a variety of systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an analytic theory for the distribution of nuclei that is formed in a nucleated pulse and then grows in a supersaturated state.
the nucleation pulse is a powerful method of generating a distribution of particles with a broad size range and with an arbitrary shape.
we have obtained a general analytic solution for the distribution function of nuclei formed in the nucleation pulse experiments, which has been tested against exact numerics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in the limit of long pulses the distribution of nuclei approaches an exponential shape, while in case of short pulses it is described in terms of a single maximum.

the distribution of nuclei produced by a nucleation pulse, which is the starting point for any nucleation-growth analysis, can exhibit a very complex behavior, and the asymptotics of this distribution depends strongly on the ratio of critical radii.
the size-distribution of the nuclei formed by a pulse is not necessarily Gaussian, but rather can be strongly skewed, depending on the duration of the pulse.
